news.Title: Google plans $17 billion Wyoming data center amid rising threats of curbs
news.Content:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Alphabet's Google will invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming, the ‌company said on Thursday, pushing ahead with a major ‌AI infrastructure investment as political resistance to data center expansion grows following ​the US midterm elections.

Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.

Google's facility will be built in partnership ‌with Tallgrass Energy, Black ⁠Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital.

The project will be powered in part by a ⁠planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell development equipped with carbon capture and storage technology. The fuel cells will be supplied by Bloom Energy.

Wyoming is ​a ​Republican stronghold, where Donald Trump ​won more than 70% of ‌the presidential vote in 2024.

The announcement comes as investors reassess the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. Wins by candidates opposed to data-center expansion in key Texas and Georgia races during the midterm elections have added to concerns that ‌political resistance could complicate the industry's ​rapid expansion.

Meanwhile, Microsoft has declined to expand ​a Texas data-center ​agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale, with Bloomberg ‌News reporting earlier in the ​day that the ​company planned to tighten oversight of some data-center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale.

Shares of Bloom ​Energy also slumped ‌more than 14% on worries that any potential restrictions ​could hit the industry.

(Reporting by Prathik Jayaprakash in ​Bengaluru; Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila)

news.Title: Why Marvell Stock Is Falling Today
news.Content:
Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL) stock is down 13.4% as of 2:42 p.m. ET on Thursday, Nov. 5, after Democrats' midterm victory set off a sell-off in chip and AI infrastructure stocks .

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) are down 3.9% and 5.0%, respectively.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why Marvell stock is falling after the midterms

Investors are fleeing anything tied to AI data centers two days after Democrats flipped both houses of the U.S. Congress and won several key governorships.

Many Democrats ran on a platform that included increased oversight of the AI industry, with the party's new governors in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia -- major AI data center states -- promising construction moratoriums.

Marvell sells the networking chips that move data around inside those data centers -- it sits right in the blast zone.

Image source: Getty Images.

How Marvell's Lumentum deal could dilute shareholders

But this comes just days after an all-stock deal was announced Monday to buy Lumentum (NASDAQ:LITE) -- an AI photonics maker -- worth $115 billion. That could lead to significant dilution for Marvell stock. But it also means that as Marvell stock drops, the value of the shares it is offering Lumentum falls as well. There's a risk the deal falls apart or the terms get renegotiated, and Marvell shareholders see even more dilution.

news.Title: Why It’s Time to Load Up on Arm Stock
news.Content:
Arm Holdings (ARM) stock fell sharply, down 44% over the past month and trading about 63% below its 52-week high. The selloff in ARM stock intensified following the company's second-quarter earnings announcement, as concerns over slowing royalty revenue growth led by the softness in the smartphone market weighed on investor sentiment. Today's broad selloff in chipmakers and AI stocks hasn't done ARM stock any favors either.

Overall, however, Arm's underlying business performance remains encouraging. Strong demand for ARM-based computing architectures helped drive solid growth in both revenue and earnings during the quarter. That said, the smartphone market continues to pose a challenge. Higher memory prices are weighing on smartphone demand, particularly in the mid- and lower-end segments, pressuring royalty revenue. Royalty revenue from edge AI applications was also broadly flat year-over-year (YoY).

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Super Micro Computer Posts Record $19.9 Billion Quarter, But 44% of Revenue Came From a Single Customer

The Oracle Selloff Deepens Despite Strong Long-Term Growth Outlook. How to Play ORCL Stock Here.

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

Management expects these challenges to persist in the near term. While demand from cloud AI and physical AI is expected to support royalty growth, continued weakness in the smartphone market and tough YoY comparisons are likely to limit gains in edge AI. As a result, Arm expects royalty revenue to increase at a low teens rate sequentially but only at a low single-digit rate YoY, pointing to a further slowdown in growth.

Nevertheless, the royalty business is only part of the investment story. Arm continues to see strong demand for its licensing portfolio, which is expected to more than offset the near-term weakness in royalties. Growing adoption of its architecture across AI, cloud computing, and other high-performance computing applications provides solid growth opportunities.

Although the slowdown in royalty revenue and weakness in smartphone demand cannot be overlooked, the recent selloff has created a more attractive risk-reward opportunity.

Arm to Sustain Solid Growth Despite Smartphone Weakness

Arm reported a strong second quarter, and momentum will likely continue. Its revenue rose 27% YoY to $1.44 billion, marking its fifth consecutive quarter of growth above 20%. Growth was largely driven by a 50% increase in licensing revenue to $773 million, reflecting stronger customer demand for Arm's technology and Compute Platform. The higher licensing activity is encouraging, as it indicates that more customers are committing to Arm's architecture, which could translate into higher royalty revenue in the future.

Story Continues

Royalty revenue increased 8% YoY to $670 million, supported by strong demand from cloud AI and physical AI markets. Data center royalties doubled from the previous year as Arm-based CPUs gained traction across AI infrastructure and cloud computing. Physical AI royalties also grew 50%, driven by wider adoption of Arm technology in automotive and robotics.

However, edge AI growth remained relatively flat as higher memory prices continued to weigh on smartphone demand. This weakness was partly offset by higher royalty rates from the growing adoption of Armv9 and its Compute Subsystems (CSS). A recovery in smartphone demand could provide further support to royalty growth over time.

Arm's bottom-line performance was also strong, with adjusted EPS increasing 33% to $0.52, outpacing revenue growth. Another positive development was the improving outlook for Arm's AGI CPU business. Management now sees the opportunity to generate up to $2 billion in revenue across FY2027 and FY2028, compared with its earlier expectation of more than $1 billion. This upbeat guidance follows new purchase orders from multiple customers and supply agreements with supply-chain partners.

Looking ahead to Q3, Arm expects revenue of approximately $1.54 billion, representing around 24% YoY growth, while adjusted EPS is projected at $0.56, up 30%. Licensing revenue is expected to remain strong, with growth above 50%. Royalty growth should continue to benefit from cloud and physical AI demand, although weaker smartphone sales and a challenging comparison base are likely to limit near-term growth.

Overall, Arm's business remains well-positioned to benefit from rising AI-related demand. While weakness in the smartphone market may weigh on near-term royalties, strong licensing activity, growing data center adoption, and contributions from AGI CPUs provide meaningful support for longer-term growth prospects.

ARM Stock's Selloff Is a Buying Opportunity

ARM stock's recent pullback has created an attractive entry point for long-term investors, despite near-term challenges in its royalty business. While persistent weakness in the smartphone market could constrain royalty growth, strong licensing demand, accelerating data center adoption, and the expanding opportunity in AGI CPUs provide multiple growth drivers.

While analysts have a "Moderate Buy" consensus rating on ARM stock, its solid fundamentals and significant share price decline make it an attractive stock to consider now.

news.Title: What Anthropic's IPO could mean for Amazon and Google
news.Content:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) is preparing for what could be a historic initial public offering (IPO) later this month, with Wall Street expecting the company to launch with a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

A public debut at the top end would put Anthropic ahead of SpaceX ( SPCX ) for the most valuable stock market IPO in history.

That would make plenty of people a whole lot richer on paper virtually overnight, including big-name investors like Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), two of the company's largest backers.

The tech giants have invested billions of dollars in Anthropic, and, according to the AI lab's amended S-1 investor prospectus , the pair will hold more than 5% of Anthropic's outstanding stock when it goes public.

But those hefty investments also carry substantial risks if the company falls short of Wall Street's enormous expectations.

"There's risk to their investment in that … who knows in five years whether Anthropic will be the most profitable company in the world — or worth nothing," Dorothy Lund, co-director of Columbia Law School's Ira M. Millstein Center for Global Markets and Corporate Ownership , told Yahoo Finance.

"There are a lot of questions."

Investors, suppliers, competitors

According to Amazon's latest quarterly filing , the company has invested $18 billion in Anthropic so far, and currently has a financing agreement with the startup worth up to an additional $15 billion.

As of Sept. 30, those investments were worth $92.5 billion in Anthropic nonvoting preferred stock. Amazon also said it holds $146.2 billion in notes, which would convert to stock when Anthropic goes public.

Google doesn't break out the exact value of individual investments, but in April it revealed plans to invest upwards of $40 billion in the company if it meets certain performance obligations . That's in addition to prior investments worth roughly $3 billion.

Anthropic and Google aren't just investors in Anthropic; they are also major compute suppliers.

In May, The Information reported that Anthropic entered into a $200 billion agreement to use Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) over a five-year period. Anthropic has also agreed to spend more than $100 billion via Amazon's AWS over the next 10 years.

That means in addition to investment gains, the cloud giants will also earn revenue on sales to Anthropic. Such deals have frequently raised concerns about circular investing, creating an unsustainable trend in the AI market.

It gets more interesting when you consider that Amazon and Google also compete with Anthropic. Google has its Google DeepMind frontier lab that develops its own AI models that go toe-to-toe with Anthropic's, and, according to Business Insider , Amazon is refocusing its AI efforts to better compete in the frontier space.

Story Continues

It all creates a strange mix for the companies.

The biggest benefit for Amazon and Google, however, could be the ability to continue selling compute capacity to Anthropic over time.

"To the extent that Anthropic is successful and meets the obligations that it has committed to for compute, that would clearly be a positive for Amazon and Alphabet," Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt explained.

But the tie-up between the companies could also raise legal concerns in the future.

"Regulators who are looking at this space might be kind of worried about the interrelationships here, [and] might not love to see competitors owning big chunks of each other," Lund said.

We'll see how this all plays out in the coming weeks and months as Anthropic speeds toward its IPO.

news.Title: Wedbush Isn’t So Sure the Marvell-Lumentum Deal Will Really Happen. Here’s Why.
news.Content:
Semiconductor giant Marvell Technology (MRVL) has pitched an acquisition of optical and photonic products manufacturer Lumentum Holdings (LITE). This brings Lumentum's lasers, optical transceivers, and optical circuit switches (OCS) to Marvell's switching, electrical and optical interconnects, and custom XPUs. While the strategic rationale is sound, investors did not like the deal.

The $115 billion all-stock acquisition announcement led to a 12.7% intraday drop in MRVL stock and an 18.6% decline in LITE stock on Nov. 2. Marvell shareholders voiced concerns about share dilution, as Lumentum holders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares per Lumentum share, leaving them with 33% of the combined company. That is expected to materially increase Marvell's share count and dilute existing holders. Lumentum shareholders are concerned because the deal would convert their ownership from a stand-alone AI optics company to Marvell shares.

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Super Micro Computer Posts Record $19.9 Billion Quarter, But 44% of Revenue Came From a Single Customer

The Oracle Selloff Deepens Despite Strong Long-Term Growth Outlook. How to Play ORCL Stock Here.

Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.

Amid all this, Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson believes the deal, set to close in the first half of 2028, might not actually happen. Beyond the regulatory approval process and China's reluctance to approve major technology mergers, lasers are in tight supply, with Lumentum currently supplying Marvell's competitors.

As the deal drives sentiment around the two stocks, let's take a closer look at them.

The One Carrying Out the Acquisition: Marvell Technology (MRVL)

Marvell is a fabless semiconductor company that designs, develops, and sells data-infrastructure chips for data centers, cloud computing, networking, storage, security, and communications. Headquartered in Wilmington, Delaware, the company has a market capitalization of $154.05 billion.

Marvell's stock has risen over the past year mainly because investors see it as a major beneficiary of hyperscalers' spending on AI data centers. Over the past 52 weeks, MRVL stock has gained 48%, while it has risen 62% year-to-date (YTD). The company's shares reached a 52-week high of $329.88 on June 18, but are down 58% from that level. However, the stock has dropped 37% over the past five days, mainly due to investor skepticism about the Lumentum deal and a broader selloff in chipmakers and AI stocks.

Story Continues

Despite the recent selloff, Marvell's stock still doesn't come cheap. On a forward-adjusted basis, its price-to-earnings (non-GAAP) ratio of 56.37x is higher than the industry average of 21.21x.

In the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (quarter ended Aug. 1), Marvell reported strong results driven by demand in its data center portfolio, in which the company reported a 46% year-over-year (YoY) growth. Its AI-related bookings remained robust, which is expected to continue creating tailwinds for its top line. Data centers now make up 79% of its revenue. The company's total revenue increased 37% YoY to $2.74 billion. Its adjusted EPS rose 40% from the prior-year period to $0.94.

Wall Street analysts are robustly optimistic about Marvell's future earnings. They expect the company's EPS to climb 27.4% YoY to $0.79 for the third quarter of fiscal 2027. For fiscal 2027, EPS is projected to surge 41.2% to $3.05, followed by a 99.7% growth to $6.09 in fiscal 2028.

Marvell is gaining praise on Wall Street, with analysts awarding it a consensus "Strong Buy" rating overall. Of the 39 analysts rating MRVL stock, 28 have given it a "Strong Buy" rating, three analysts rated it a "Moderate Buy," and eight took a middle-of-the-road approach with a "Hold" rating. The consensus price target of $317.05 represents an 131% upside from current levels. The Street-high price target of $450 implies a 229% upside.

The One Being Acquired: Lumentum Holdings (LITE)

Lumentum designs and manufactures optical and photonic technologies, including high-performance lasers, modules, and optical subsystems. Its products support data-center connectivity for AI and cloud computing, telecommunications networks, industrial manufacturing, and sensing applications. Headquartered in San Jose, California, Lumentum operates research, manufacturing, and sales facilities worldwide. The company has a market capitalization of $61.68 billion.

Due to explosive AI optics demand, Lumentum's stock has gained 126% over the past 52 weeks, while it has been up 43% YTD. Like Marvell, Lumentum's stock is also deep in the red, down 43% over the past five days due to both the same skepticism regarding the deal and the aforementioned broader selloff hitting most AI-related stocks. LITE stock reached a 52-week high of $1,143 on Oct. 9, but is down 54% from that level.

On a forward-adjusted basis, Lumentum's stock has a price-to-earnings (non-GAAP) ratio of 34.36x, which is higher than the industry average of 21.21x.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (quarter ended Sept. 26), Lumentum reported growth across all businesses, with pump lasers and OCS being the leading contributors. The company also reported greater OCS demand visibility, positioning optical switching as a multi-billion-dollar annual revenue stream. The company's total revenue increased 136.5% YoY to $1.26 billion, while its non-GAAP EPS increased from $1.10 to $4.57 over the same period.

Wall Street analysts are strongly optimistic about Lumentum's future earnings trajectory. They expect the company's EPS to climb 271% YoY to $4.60 for the current quarter. For fiscal 2027, EPS is projected to surge 143.5% to $19.80, followed by a 67.8% growth to $33.23 in fiscal 2028.

Lumentum's stock has become a popular name on Wall Street, with analysts awarding it a consensus "Moderate Buy" rating. Of the 25 analysts rating LITE stock, 17 analysts have rated it a "Strong Buy," one analyst rated it a "Moderate Buy," and seven analysts gave a "Hold" rating. The consensus price target of $1,094.72 represents a 107% upside from current levels. Moreover, the Street-high price target of $1,500 indicates a 184% upside.

news.Title: Google Plans to Spend $17 Billion on Wyoming Data Center
news.Content:
(Bloomberg) -- Alphabet Inc.'s Google will spend $17 billion to build a data center in Wyoming, formally putting a price tag on the proposal two days after voters across the US delivered a broad rebuke to the development of such massive projects for artificial intelligence work.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal

Democrats Clinch Huge Wins on Inflation Anger, Trump Fatigue

S&P 500 Sinks 4% as AI Washout Rattles Wall Street: Markets Wrap

What the Democrats' Sweep of Congress Means for Trump

Trump Now Has to Govern Through a Midterm Meltdown of His Own Making

Voters in Tuesday's US midterm elections sided with limits on data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, according to Ballotpedia. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor's race after promising a data center moratorium. Successful Democratic candidates for governor in Georgia, Ohio and Pennsylvania also campaigned on stricter regulations of these projects.

Google said Thursday in a blog post that the facility in Laramie County, Wyoming, will be its first in the state. The company said it will pay for all the power the data center uses. Last month, American Electric Power Co. said it planned to invest $4 billion in the project, which will draw electricity in part from a 702-megawatt natural gas fuel cell development built with Bloom Energy Corp. fuel cells, and will be air-cooled to limit water use.

The deal reflects growing interest from technology companies in Bloom's fuel cells as they look to provide power for energy-hungry AI systems. Natural gas turbines are back-ordered for years, and nuclear projects can take a decade or more to permit and build. Bloom says its fuel cells can be installed in as little as 90 days.

Google also said it expects to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in local property taxes and will form a Community Council with its partners to address growth concerns in Cheyenne, Wyoming.

Bloomberg reported in June that data center developer Crusoe had been pushed aside at the site after Google raised concerns about the costs and timetable, according to people familiar with the situation. Energy utility Black Hills Corp., which had been working to line up agreements to power the project, said it was moving forward without Crusoe. Google on Thursday named Black Hills Energy as a partner in the Wyoming project.

Crusoe initially announced the Wyoming project in July 2025, alongside the Blackstone Inc.-backed infrastructure firm Tallgrass. At the time, Crusoe Chief Executive Officer Chase Lochmiller said the complex would eventually be capable of scaling up to 10 gigawatts. Tallgrass Energy was named a partner in Google's announcement. A gigawatt of electricity is enough to power 750,000 US homes at any one time.

news.Title: Don’t Rush to Buy the Dip in Neocloud Stocks. Microsoft’s Cold Feet Could Be a Bigger Problem Than the Blue Wave.
news.Content:
The neocloud group is selling off again today, pressured by two converging forces — a Bloomberg report that Microsoft (MSFT) has "buyer's remorse" over its massive investments in data center operators, and sweeping Democratic midterm victories that threaten to slow the pace of U.S. data center construction. IREN (IREN) is plunging 16%, CoreWeave (CRWV) is falling 11%, and Nebius (NBIS) is cratering 15%, with the neocloud stocks taking part in a broader tech sector plunge.

"[Microsoft] is tightening oversight of some data center projects from Nebius Group NV, IREN Ltd., and Nscale Plc, stepping away from ones it deems risky and debating internally whether to ink new neocloud deals, according to people familiar with the matter," according to Bloomberg's reporting.

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Super Micro Computer Posts Record $19.9 Billion Quarter, But 44% of Revenue Came From a Single Customer

The Oracle Selloff Deepens Despite Strong Long-Term Growth Outlook. How to Play ORCL Stock Here.

Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.

Microsoft Is Getting Selective With AI Infrastructure

Microsoft's CFO confirmed on last week's earnings call that third-party capacity deliveries expected in the September quarter were delayed, and reporting has specifically linked IREN's Childress site to the shortfall.

IREN's multiyear contract with Microsoft is valued at $9.7 billion, and investors will scrutinize tonight's fiscal first-quarter report for whether its remaining three 50-megawatt GPU deployments stay on track for December delivery.

Microsoft also reportedly declined an option to expand its lease with Nscale, another neocloud provider, which reinforces the narrative that the dominant hyperscaler is becoming dramatically more selective with its AI infrastructure commitments.

Texas Moratorium Threatens 27% of U.S. Data Center Capacity

The political dimension is equally consequential, as Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged an immediate moratorium on new data center approvals in a state that Wells Fargo estimates accounts for roughly 27% of planned U.S. data center capacity. Voters across at least 40 of 41 local ballot measures nationwide sided against data center development, signaling broad grassroots opposition that extends well beyond a single state.

UBS analysts estimate roughly 30% of expected 2028 U.S. data center capacity additions could be at risk from construction pauses, while Goldman Sachs puts the share of planned capacity in states likely to face new restrictions at approximately 45% — a striking gap that underscores the uncertainty.

Story Continues

Three Stocks, Three Very Different Risk Profiles

Among some of the top publicly traded neocloud stocks cited in the Bloomberg reporting, IREN is the most directly exposed name politically because it operates two Texas campuses and is specifically cited in the Microsoft spending shortfall, with its fiscal 2027 EPS estimates collapsing to negative $3.42 from negative $0.94 just 60 days ago and revenue missing consensus in each of the past four quarters.

CoreWeave carries the heaviest financial burden, with total debt reaching $51.6 billion by mid-2026 and second-quarter interest expense of $640 million swamping its $128 million of adjusted operating income — a gap so wide that its bonds now trade near distressed levels around 80 cents on the dollar, with credit default swap spreads at record highs.

Nebius, by contrast, carries a far lighter $10 billion debt load, funds growth largely through customer prepayments and equity issuance rather than leveraged borrowing, and has no disclosed Texas sites, though concentration risk remains elevated with three customers accounting for 59% of second-quarter revenue.

Valuations Have Cratered, But Is It Enough?

Valuation compression has been dramatic across all three names, with Nebius trading at roughly 5 times forward sales — half its five-year average of approximately 11 times — CoreWeave sitting at 3.5 times trailing revenue versus a peer average above 10 times, and IREN at just over 2 times book value with analyst price targets averaging $72, more than triple the current price, though such targets typically lag steep selloffs.

The question is whether these discounts adequately compensate for execution risk, regulatory uncertainty, and, in CoreWeave's case, a balance sheet where the debt-to-equity ratio exceeds 8.9.

Don't Assume the Bottom Is In

Even deeply oversold conditions do not guarantee a swift recovery when policy headlines from newly installed state leaders, upcoming earnings reports — IREN tonight, CoreWeave on November 10, Nebius on November 12 — and macro data including Friday's October payrolls report will continue to generate outsized volatility.

CoreWeave looks to be the most precarious of the group, as even a strong operating quarter may not resolve the structural concern that its quarterly interest bill of $860–940 million dwarfs what operations actually earn. Until adjusted operating income demonstrably closes that gap, the equity remains subordinated to a massive debt stack — a problem no single earnings beat can fix.

news.Title: Is Arm Holdings a Buy After Its Latest Earnings Report?
news.Content:
Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) delivered a record fiscal second quarter, yet its stock has fallen approximately 11.5% as of noon following yesterday's earnings report.

That's an uncomfortable reaction for a company reporting 27% revenue growth, a 33% increase in adjusted earnings and a 50% surge in licensing revenue.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Why is Wall Street selling?

On paper, the AI growth story remains firmly intact. But investors aren't simply buying visible growth anymore. They're demanding evidence that today's AI spending will translate into sustainable earnings and cash flow.

There seems to be an important disconnect between Arm's operating performance and investor expectations. Second-quarter revenue reached $1.44 billion, while data center royalties doubled year-over-year. Management also raised its optimism, now expecting its new AGI CPU — Arm's first production chip to specifically assist agentic AI — to generate up to $2 billion in cumulative revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

But here's where the analysis gets interesting. Licensing and other revenue surged 50% to $773 million, but the Annualized Contract Value (ACV), a better indicator of underlying licensing momentum, grew just 12%. Wall Street seems to be focusing on this divergence.

Large licensing agreements can inflate quarterly revenue, but they don't automatically produce recurring royalties. Customers of Arm's proprietary technology must still design, manufacture, and ship chips before Arm collects those payments.

The metric investors must focus on

It's easy for investors to look at the $773 million in licensing revenue and its 50% growth and assume the business is accelerating.

But Annualized Contract Value (ACV) growth of just 12% is disappointing, and that's the metric investors must keep a close eye on. ACV essentially strips out much of the quarterly noise from large licensing agreements, providing a clearer picture of underlying licensing momentum.

The uncomfortable truth is that while reported licensing growth grew 50%, underlying ACV growth actually slowed.

This doesn't mean Arm's business is deteriorating. It means the headline number looks more attractive than the underlying core driver.

The divergence becomes obvious when we put the last three quarters side by side:

The real investment question isn't whether Arm can book another massive licensing quarter. It's whether those customer commitments become production designs, shipped chips, and recurring royalties.

Arm Holdings signed several large licensing agreements and benefited from the timing and accounting treatment of those deals. The resulting revenue hit the income statement immediately, but the underlying annualized contract base didn't expand nearly as quickly.

Meanwhile, customers continue to invest in Arm technology. More than 60 active ATA subscriptions and additional CSS agreements support the longer-term opportunity. But investors should not mistake upfront licensing revenue for guaranteed future royalties.

Here's the operational reality: Arm licenses technology first. Customers spend months designing chips. Manufacturers then produce those chips. Only when production ramps do recurring royalties follow.

Valuation has little room for error

Arm's business is firing on multiple cylinders, but its valuation leaves very little room for disappointment. Even after the recent 11% sell-off, investors are still paying an extraordinary premium for the company's future growth.

ARM PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts .

As of noon, Arm shares trade at approximately 173 times trailing earnings and more than 75 times forward earnings. That kind of valuation is too large and risky to justify.

Such a premium assumes Arm can successfully convert its licensing momentum into recurring royalties, capture a meaningful share of the AI server CPU market, and scale its AGI CPU business without sacrificing profitability. That's a lot of execution already embedded in the share price.

The risks are not hypothetical. Royalty growth of 8% lagged the explosive licensing performance. AGI CPU shipments have yet to ramp materially; initial gross margins are expected to be just 30–40%, and supply-chain constraints remain an obstacle. Meanwhile, competition from rival chip companies AMD and Intel isn't going away.

Is the stock a buy?

ARM is a compelling long-term business, but at this valuation, I don't see much upside anytime soon. I'd rather remain on the sidelines than chase the AI narrative. Today's decline makes the stock cheaper, but not necessarily cheap in the absolute sense.

I'd rather wait for a more attractive entry point or another quarter confirming that licensing commitments are converting into royalties and AGI shipments.

But, at the end of the day, there's no prize for buying a great company at any price. Arm deserves a place on the watch list, but until valuation catches up with fundamentals, patience may be the better investment strategy.

news.Title: Dear TeraWulf Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 6
news.Content:
TeraWulf (WULF) builds, owns, and runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers for hyperscalers, and right now that is a punishing business to be in. The past month has been an absolute bloodbath for neocloud and AI data center stocks, and TeraWulf has taken its share of the damage, with shares down double digits. The pressure is coming from two directions.

At home, TeraWulf faces a heavy construction-funding risk. Across the sector, investors are dumping AI data center stocks as anxiety builds over heavy leverage, negative free cash flow, and tightening debt markets. Even a major vote of confidence couldn't stop the slide. On Nov. 4, Alphabet's (GOOG) (GOOGL) Google guaranteed $19 billion in long-term Anthropic leases at TeraWulf's Kentucky AI data center campus, a headline that should have sparked a rally. Instead, the WULF stock slid about 6.6% and then nosedived even further the next day by 14%.

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Pays Warren Buffett's Berkshire $848 Million a Year as Jim Cramer Says Buy KO Stock

Super Micro Computer Posts Record $19.9 Billion Quarter, But 44% of Revenue Came From a Single Customer

The Oracle Selloff Deepens Despite Strong Long-Term Growth Outlook. How to Play ORCL Stock Here.

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

The reason is timing. The financial backstop and lease guarantee only kick in after each data hall is finished, so until then, TeraWulf is the one footing the bill. It carries the near-term capital expenditure and funding weight through the entire building phase, and investors are clearly worried about whether the money holds out. That makes the next few days critical. TeraWulf reports its fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings before the market opens on Friday, Nov. 6. So, with the stock under pressure and nerves running high, here's a closer look at TeraWulf.

About TeraWulf Stock

Founded in 2021, TeraWulf develops, owns, and operates large-scale, power-backed digital infrastructure across the United States, purpose-built to support high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence workloads. The company leverages long-term control over land, power, and interconnection infrastructure, backed by deep in-house expertise in energy markets, infrastructure development, and data center operations.

TeraWulf currently operates the Lake Mariner Data Campus in New York while developing and pursuing additional large-scale campuses across Kentucky, New York, and Maryland. Alongside its HPC and AI ambitions, the company also operates existing Bitcoin-mining infrastructure at Lake Mariner, portions of which are being repurposed to accommodate contracted HPC development.

Story Continues

With a market capitalization of approximately $5.84 billion, TeraWulf has had a turbulent run on Wall Street, with shares struggling to regain momentum. The stock has plunged 33% over the past year and is down 11% in 2026. By comparison, the broader S&P 500 Index ($SPX) has gained 9.5% over the past year and 8.7% so far in 2026. The selloff has intensified in recent weeks, with WULF shares tumbling almost 31% over the past month alone.

Inside TeraWulf's Q2 Earnings Report

TeraWulf's second-quarter 2026 results published in early August underscored a dramatic shift in its business model, as the company accelerated its transition away from traditional cryptocurrency mining and doubled down on high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure for artificial intelligence. During the quarter, revenue came in at $44.78 million, with HPC lease revenue contributing $31.93 million, or approximately 71% of total sales.

This growing contribution firmly established data center hosting as the company's primary revenue driver, highlighting the progress of its strategic pivot. However, the transition came with significant near-term profitability pressures as expansion costs mounted. TeraWulf reported a massive GAAP net loss of $939.92 million, largely driven by non-operating accounting adjustments.

Meanwhile, operating expenses surged as the company expanded its corporate infrastructure to support its multi-gigawatt development pipeline, dragging adjusted EBITDA to negative $18.3 million. The cost burden was also evident in the company's expense structure. Selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses climbed to $112.4 million, while interest expenses reached $56.4 million, reflecting the substantial overhead and financing demands of transforming a bitcoin (BTCUSD) miner into an institutional-grade neocloud infrastructure provider.

Loss per share widened to $1.94 from just $0.05 in the year-ago quarter. Nevertheless, TeraWulf ended the quarter with approximately $3 billion in cash and restricted cash, providing a substantial liquidity cushion to support contracted projects and future expansion. Beyond the financial performance, the quarter laid the groundwork for several significant growth catalysts, particularly the company's push into long-term hyperscale data center agreements.

With 102 MW of operational IT capacity at Lake Mariner and another 336 MW under construction, TeraWulf was positioning itself for a major expansion in HPC hosting. This momentum culminated in its landmark 20-year, 401 MW lease agreement with Anthropic. The company also entered into an agreement to sell its entire 50.1% stake in the Abernathy Joint Venture for approximately $530 million in cash, further strengthening its strategic and financial position.

What Do Analysts Think About WULF Stock?

Wall Street remains firmly bullish on TeraWulf, with the stock commanding a consensus "Strong Buy" rating. Of the 26 analysts covering WULF stock, 21 recommend "Strong Buy," three assign "Moderate Buy," one maintains a "Hold," and one issues a "Strong Sell." The average price target of $30.16 points to a potential upside of approximately 200%, while the Street-high target of $65 suggests a staggering 547% upside from current levels.

news.Title: Neocloud Stocks Fell More Than Hyperscalers After Election Night. Here's Why Exposure Differs.
news.Content:
On Nov. 3, the Democrats swept the House and Senate in the U.S. midterm elections. They also flipped the governorships of five states -- Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas -- from red to blue. That outcome was grim news for the booming AI market, since many Democrats support tighter restrictions on the construction of new data centers.

That's why it wasn't surprising when many top neocloud stocks -- including CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) and Nebius (NASDAQ: NBIS) -- dropped after election night. Yet the top hyperscaler stocks -- Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) -- rallied. Let's see why that happened, and if that divergence will continue for the foreseeable future.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why did the neocloud stocks stumble?

Neocloud companies buy and lease data centers, load them up with Nvidia 's top-tier GPUs, and rent that computing power to other companies. By providing only raw GPU power, these companies can process AI tasks more efficiently than larger cloud infrastructure platforms, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure.

However, most of these neocloud companies are unprofitable, yet they're taking on more debt and issuing more shares to buy or lease new data centers and GPUs. That strategy works as long as the AI market continues to expand, regulators don't actively block the construction of new data centers, and interest rates remain stable.

But today, the macro headwinds could drive more companies to rein in their AI spending; the Democrats (and some Republicans) could actively block new data center projects, and the Fed -- which already raised its benchmark rates for the first time in three years this September -- could implement more rate hikes if inflation doesn't cool off.

CoreWeave, Nebius, and other neocloud companies are still growing rapidly, but they're racking up steep losses and taking on significant leverage.

CoreWeave ended the second quarter of 2026 with $72 billion in total liabilities, a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3, and an average yield to maturity of 14.1% to 15.6% on its senior unsecured bonds. Analysts still expect its revenue to surge 151% in 2026 and 106% in 2027, but they're probably not sure if it can stay solvent if interest rates keep rising and the AI market cools off.

Story Continues

That's why the top neocloud stocks sank after the election, and why Elon Musk recently predicted the industry could face a "guppy-level death and consolidation" in the near future.

Why did the hyperscaler stocks soar?

Amazon, Microsoft, and other hyperscalers are also aggressively expanding their cloud and AI infrastructure. Some of them -- including Microsoft and Meta -- are even renting capacity from neocloud companies to supplement their massive AI demands.

In theory, tighter data center regulations, higher interest rates, and slower AI spending could potentially hurt these hyperscalers. However, hyperscalers like Amazon and Microsoft are also profitable, have ample liquidity, and are well diversified across other industries.

Amazon generates most of its revenue from its retail business, while most of its profits come from AWS. AWS has certainly benefited from the AI market's rapid expansion, but it also provides cloud storage and compute to a wide range of non-AI industries.

Microsoft relies on Azure for most of its growth, but its business is also diversified across enterprise software, PC hardware, and gaming. It's also using AI to cut costs (by automating more jobs) rather than simply increasing its spending to expand its AI infrastructure.

Moreover, tighter data center restrictions might make top hyperscaler stocks more appealing in two ways. First, they could drive them to reduce their capex (which has soared over the past two years) by throttling their aggressive expansion plans. Second, those restrictions could make it harder for smaller cloud infrastructure companies to catch up to the market leaders.

That's why hyperscaler stocks jumped after the election, while neocloud stocks stumbled. I believe that trend will continue until we get a clearer idea of where the Democratic majority plans to steer the broader AI and data center markets.

news.Title: Why Arm Holdings Stock Is Crashing Today
news.Content:
By most measures, the stock should be well up today. The company's record-breaking revenue of $1.44 billion in fiscal Q2 was not only up 27% year over year, but handily topped estimates of $1.38 billion. Earnings improved 33% to $0.52 per share as well, versus a consensus of $0.47. Guidance for the quarter currently underway was healthy too, suggesting top-line growth of 24%.

Nevertheless, as of 12:21 p.m. ET, shares of Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) are down 11.7%, bringing their week-to-date loss to 18%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What gives?

It may be more about the market environment right now than not. But, Arm's second-quarter numbers and third-quarter outlook dished out some degree of disappointment. Taking a cue from other tumbling technology stocks , investors are selling this one too.

Arm Holdings' red flags

Chief among the red flags behind today's sizable sell-off is Arm Holdings' Q2 royalty revenue. While licensing revenue soared 50% to $773 million, royalty revenue only improved by 8% to $670 million, reflecting softness in smartphone memory prices that could linger for the foreseeable future.

This weak royalty number prompted Barclays to lower its price target on ARM from $360 per share to $325, while Goldman Sachs reiterated its sell rating and $160 price target -- compared to the stock's present price near $165 -- on the same concern.

That said, although Arm Holdings' third-quarter revenue guidance of $1.54 billion (+/- $50 million) is technically better than the analyst consensus of $1.53 billion, investors may have been tacitly expecting a stronger growth outlook from the company itself.

Image source: Getty Images.

Perhaps more than anything, however, much of today's selling can be attributed to the sweeping reset most chipmakers' stocks are suffering right now. Shares of Nvidia , Micron , and Qualcomm are also all similarly in the red on Thursday, making it easier for investors to throw in the towel on ARM.

Opportunity knocks (if you can stomach the volatility)

There are real reasons for this sweeping sell-off, to be clear. For instance, Qualcomm's fiscal fourth-quarter handset revenue fell 26%, and guidance for the fiscal first-quarter now underway was lackluster. Other chip companies are seeing similar headwinds.

This correction was inevitable sooner or later, though. It's also the beginning of a buying opportunity, even if we're not necessarily at the exact bottom yet. Just watch out for volatility, which is likely to linger even after the bottom is made and we're on the way back up.

news.Title: Sick of Swings? Same… But History Is on Our Side
news.Content:
The Nasdaq Composite is down more than 4% on Thursday as we write this. Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence (AI) trade, especially chipmakers and data center names, are sliding for a second day, both here and in Asia.

Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) has fallen sharply after its smartphone chip sales came in below expectations. Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) is lower despite reporting record revenue, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is adding to Wednesday's 7% drop.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The Nasdaq is still below its record close on Oct. 6. And if you own AI-linked stocks, including many we've recommended, this week alone may have felt like whiplash. Monday brought another drop. On Tuesday night, stock futures fell as election results came in. Wednesday brought relief. This morning, the red is back.

That's a lot to sit through, whether you started with $1,000 in a few stocks or have built a seven-figure portfolio over decades. Either way, the past month has tested our patience.

TMF co-founder and CEO Tom Gardner has never pretended this part is easy. After his October Quarterly Call, he told members he's "happy to give up fractions of future gains for stability." Even he will trade a little return for some peace of mind.

How Fast the Mood Can Turn

Tuesday night showed how quickly things can change. Stock futures fell at first as results came in, then turned higher overnight.

By Wednesday's close, the Dow had jumped 3%. That was its biggest gain the day after a midterm election since 1982, according to CFRA Research.

Picture selling your stocks at 10 p.m. on Tuesday. By Wednesday's close, you'd likely have missed the rally. Today's drop may tempt some of us to make that same mistake.

Co-founder David Gardner has a line for moments like this: "Stocks always go down faster than they go up, but they always go up more than they go down." The drops feel worse because they come so fast. Historically, though, the gains have been bigger.

Owning many stocks makes those drops easier to live through. The Motley Fool now suggests the average member own at least 50, built up over time. With that many businesses across different industries, it's much harder for any single bad morning to sink you.

AI Isn't One Trade

Not every AI stock joined Wednesday's rally. Cloud giants like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) jumped. Chipmakers fell, and so did many companies tied to the data center build-out, such as Vertiv (NYSE:VRT), GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV), and Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE). That happened even as most stocks rose.

Story Continues

If you own a cloud giant, Wednesday may have felt great. If you own a chipmaker, you may have watched your stock slide while nearly everything else climbed. That can feel lonely.

But a few rough days for a stock say little about the business behind it. Big tech companies are still spending heavily on AI, and demand for chips still looks strong. Order books at many data center suppliers also appear to be growing fast, though the ride may stay bumpy. If the companies you own keep growing, short-term swings like this one tend to matter less over time.

"AI stocks" covers very different businesses with different risks, so they won't always move together.

That's why it can help to own a mix of AI businesses, not just one kind. When one part of the trade struggles, another may be holding up.

Two Ways to Stay in the Game

If today's drop has you itching to act, two habits can help. They apply just as well whether you're investing $300 or $30,000.

First, aim to hold for at least three to five years as a minimum. One rough week, or even one disappointing quarter, tells you little about where a business will be by then. When you think in years, an overnight futures move gets much easier to ignore.

Second, keep new bets small. Try a small position in an idea that interests you. If it works out, great. If it doesn't, you've learned something without putting much of your long-term plan at risk.

The Long View

The past month has been uncomfortable, and the swings may not be over yet. We won't pretend otherwise.

But it helps to zoom out. Over the long run, the stock market has historically climbed up and to the right. Since 1874, U.S. stocks have returned about 11% in an average year, counting dividends, according to our research . Past performance does not guarantee future results. Still, that history includes wars, recessions, crashes, and plenty of months like this one.

The Motley Fool's goal is to help you beat the market over time, with a portfolio you don't lose sleep over and actually enjoy owning. That's the goal for us individually, too.

news.Title: Big Tech's massive AI spending is causing another problem for investors
news.Content:
The bottom-line-padding, stock-price-fueling stock buyback from hyperscalers may now be on pause as they spend aggressively on AI infrastructure.

Combined capital expenditures for Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle are tracking toward approximately $800 billion in 2026.

This unprecedented infrastructure sprint is fueled by aggressive investments in power generation, data centers, and advanced AI accelerators.

news.Title: Microsoft Just Walked Away From a Huge AI Deal
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ) has decided not to expand a major AI computing agreement with UK startup Nscale, walking away from an option that could have been worth tens of billions of dollars .

The decision affects additional capacity at a Texas data center where Microsoft already has a contract with Nscale. Importantly, the existing agreement remains in place. Microsoft's decision not to exercise the expansion option was made several months ago, before Nscale filed for an IPO in September.

Investor Takeaway

I think the most important point is that this does not necessarily mean Microsoft is pulling back from AI spending broadly .

The company is declining an optional expansion with one infrastructure provider. Its existing Nscale Texas contract remains intact.

That makes this look more like a project-specific discipline story than clear evidence of weakening AI demand.

For Nscale, however, the timing is difficult.

The company is trying to support a planned IPO reportedly valued around $35 billion , while investors are already questioning the financing needs and execution risk surrounding AI infrastructure businesses.

For investors, the key things to watch are whether Nscale quickly replaces Microsoft with another customer, whether Anthropic expands its relationship, financing progress in West Virginia, and whether Microsoft makes similar cuts with other AI infrastructure partners .

One rejected option does not break the AI spending boom.

But for Nscale, it raises the pressure considerably.

news.Title: MKSI Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on Strong Semiconductor Growth

Growth was driven by robust demand across Semiconductor and Electronics & Packaging, supported by AI-related investments. Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 30.7%, reflecting improved operating leverage and stronger profitability.

MKSI's Q3 Revenue Mix Strengthens

Product revenues, which accounted for 89.5% of total revenues, increased 47% year over year to $1.26 billion. The performance reflected strong demand across the company's semiconductor, electronics and packaging, and specialty industrial end markets.

Services revenues totaled $149 million, representing 10.5% of revenues. The figure increased 16.4% from the year-ago quarter, contributing to the company's broad-based top-line growth.

The new always-on CoCo and CoWork Bots autonomously execute tasks, requiring human intervention only for critical decisions or approvals.

Additional capabilities include Cortex Sandboxes, Agent Abuse Detection and Dynamic Model Routing. news.Title: AI Data Center Boom Runs Into a Political Wall
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

The U.S. midterm elections may have created a much tougher regulatory environment for new AI data centers, according to Needham, raising the risk that the next phase of the infrastructure boom becomes slower, more expensive, and more politically complicated.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with META.

Is META fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Needham said the election results produced a hostile regulatory backdrop for new data-center construction, particularly after Democrats gained control of Congress and won several key governorships, including Texas.

That matters because Texas is one of the most important locations in the current AI infrastructure buildout.

Opposition to data centers has increasingly centered on electricity prices, water usage, environmental impact, tax incentives, and whether local communities are being forced to absorb infrastructure costs . Reuters reported that data-center opponents were among the major beneficiaries of the midterm results, including candidates who campaigned on moratoriums or tighter development rules.

The election also showed that the backlash is not limited to one state.

A large number of local ballot measures moved toward restrictions, moratoriums, or tougher operating requirements, signaling that permitting risk is becoming a much broader issue for developers.

But Needham sees an important twist.

Tighter regulation could actually benefit established hyperscalers such as Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ), Alphabet ( NASDAQ:GOOG ), and Meta ( NASDAQ:META ) .

If new projects become harder to approve, existing permitted capacity becomes more valuable. Slower construction could also reduce future capital-spending estimates without immediately hurting revenue from data centers that are already operating, potentially improving near-term returns on invested capital.

Needham also argues that the biggest hyperscalers are better positioned than newer AI infrastructure companies to navigate political opposition because they have more experience, deeper resources, and stronger government-relations capabilities.

Investor Takeaway

I think the most interesting part of Needham's call is that bad news for data-center construction may not be equally bad for every AI company .

For newer developers, tighter permitting means delays, higher costs, and potentially stranded projects.

For Amazon, Google, and Meta, the same restrictions could make their already-built capacity more valuable while also giving them an excuse to slow capital spending.

Story Continues

That creates a potential shift in the AI trade.

Investors may begin valuing scarce permitted capacity just as highly as future growth plans.

For investors, the key things to watch are state moratoriums, local permitting rules, power-cost policies, hyperscaler capex revisions, and whether projects migrate toward friendlier states or overseas markets .

The AI race still needs more compute.

The political permission to build it may now be the scarcer asset.

news.Title: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold AXTI Stock After Its Strong Q3 Results?
news.Content:
AXT, Inc. AXTI is emerging as a key beneficiary of AI data-center networking upgrades following a breakout third quarter. Revenues climbed 162% year over year to a record $73.4 million, while non-GAAP earnings swung to 41 cents per share from a loss of 3 cents a year earlier. Non-GAAP gross margin jumped to 56.1% from 22.4%, reflecting higher indium phosphide (InP) volumes, favorable product mix and improved manufacturing productivity.

However, the stock's remarkable rally has raised the bar for further gains. AXTI has surged 190.8% year to date compared with an 11.4% rise for the Zacks Electronics – Semiconductors industry and a 9.1% gain for the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector.

AXTI stock has also outperformed several major semiconductor peers, including Marvell Technology MRVL, FormFactor FORM and Amkor Technology AMKR. Year to date, shares of Marvell Technology have jumped 88.1% and FormFactor has advanced 52.9%, while Amkor Technology has declined 9.6%.

YTD Price Return Performance

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Such outperformance raises an important question: Is AXTI still worth buying at current levels, or should investors book profits or continue holding the stock? Let's take a closer look at its growth prospects, valuation and key risks.

AXTI's InP Franchise and Capacity Expansion Underpin Growth

AXTI's InP sales reached $54.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, representing roughly 74% of revenues. Its substrates support lasers and photodetectors used in 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers, increasingly important as AI clusters demand faster interconnects.

Demand for high-quality InP substrates remains ahead of supply, providing AXTI with considerable growth opportunities. The company surpassed its initial 2026 capacity-doubling goal in August and is progressing toward larger 4-inch and 6-inch substrates. Advanced crystal-growth furnaces and low-defect materials could lift output, selling prices and margins.

Backlog surpassed $500 million, spanning multiyear agreements, shorter contracts and spot orders. A Lumentum supply agreement brought a $43.5 million wafer prepayment, strengthening demand visibility; importantly, the payment remains a liability until shipments occur. Management aims to double InP capacity again in 2027, backed by investments in raw-material sourcing and production efficiency.

AXTI's technological positioning also differentiates it within the semiconductor supply chain. Marvell Technology develops optical DSPs that enable high-speed links, FormFactor supplies semiconductor testing solutions and Amkor Technology provides semiconductor packaging and testing services. While all three companies can benefit from AI infrastructure investments, AXTI's exposure to specialized InP substrate production gives it a more concentrated opportunity tied to optical connectivity.

Story Continues

AXTI's Earnings Outlook Signals Growth

For the fourth quarter of 2026, AXTI expects non-GAAP EPS of 57-59 cents and GAAP EPS of 56-58 cents. Management also anticipates generating approximately $90 million in revenues from substrate products and raw materials for which export permits have already been secured or are not required.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for AXTI's fourth-quarter 2026 earnings is pegged at 56 cents per share, compared with a loss of 5 cents a year ago. The full-year 2026 EPS consensus stands at $1.17 per share, followed by $2.47 for 2027, indicating significant growth. The consensus estimates have moved higher over the past 30 and 60 days, signaling improving analyst expectations.

China Exposure and Capacity Execution Remain Risks

Most of AXTI's manufacturing operations are based in China, making export permits and U.S.-China tensions material swing factors. Shipments requiring additional approvals may be delayed even when demand is strong. The company must also execute a rapid capacity ramp without sacrificing yields, while rising raw-material costs could pressure profitability. Backlog includes spot orders and shorter commitments, so it is not equivalent to guaranteed revenues.

Growth also brings financing and ownership trade-offs. The diluted weighted-average share count increased to 65.9 million in the reported third quarter from 43.8 million a year earlier. A planned investment of up to $545 million into subsidiary Tongmei would finance expansion but, if fully completed, lower AXT's ownership to approximately 73.4%. Compared with Marvell Technology's broader product portfolio, FormFactor's test-equipment exposure and Amkor Technology's packaging footprint, AXTI is particularly sensitive to InP production and export constraints.

AXTI's Rich Valuation Raises the Bar

AXTI's valuation presents a significant hurdle for investors. The stock trades at 24.43X forward 12-month Price/Earnings (P/E) compared with 8.77X for the Zacks Electronics – Semiconductors industry, representing approximately 2.8 times the industry's valuation multiple. AXTI also carries a Value Score of F, indicating overvaluation relative to fundamentals.

This premium is particularly notable following the stock's 193% year-to-date appreciation. While strong earnings growth and the expanding InP opportunity provide fundamental support, much of AXTI's anticipated growth may already be reflected in its share price. Consequently, any delays in export approvals, capacity expansion or wafer-yield improvements could weigh on investor sentiment and put pressure on the stock's valuation.

AXTI's P/E Ratio (F12M)

Conclusion: Hold AXTI Stock

AXTI's record profitability, accelerating InP demand, expanding production capacity and substantial backlog support a compelling multiyear growth narrative. The company's stronger fourth-quarter earnings guidance and continued investment in larger-diameter substrates further strengthen the company's long-term prospects.

Nevertheless, export dependence, share dilution, capacity-ramp uncertainty and a sizable valuation premium argue against chasing the stock after its 193% surge. Investors may consider holding AXTI while monitoring export approvals, 4-inch and 6-inch production yields, backlog conversion and actual earnings-estimate revisions for further gains.

AXTI currently has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here .

news.Title: Microsoft Stock Has Gained More Than 50% in About 4 Months. Here's What It Has Usually Done Next.
news.Content:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) shares jumped nearly 7% on Wednesday, Nov. 4, as U.S. stocks rallied the day after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections.

The stock sits near $553 as of this writing. That leaves it about 57% over its June 25 close of $352.83, and the rise took just 92 trading days.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

A move like that is rare for a company worth about $4 trillion. But Microsoft has done it before. Going back through its daily closing prices to 1986, I find 13 past runs like this one. In 11 of them, the stock was up a year later, with a median one-year gain of around 33%.

It's a solid record. But it might mean less than it seems. Microsoft stock has climbed in around 74% of all one-year periods since 1986, fast run or not. And the latest run, in July 2025, is one of the two that finished down.

Image source: Getty Images.

Most of the big years came early

Every run starts the first day Microsoft closed at least 50% over its lowest close in the past 92 trading days. I used split-adjusted prices without dividends, and runs had to begin at least one year apart. "A year later" is the close 12 months after a run started (or the last trading day before it). By this rule, the current run began on Oct. 6.

Ten of the 13 past runs came between 1986 and 2001, when Microsoft was a much smaller company. The biggest years came in that stretch, too. Shares more than doubled over the year after the runs that began in November 1986, January 1991, and March 1998.

The one early miss followed a January 1988 run, when the stock was recovering from the October 1987 crash, and shares were around 12% down a year later.

Since the 2001 run, Microsoft has only moved this fast three times. The stock gained around 12% over the year after June 2009 and about 33% after June 2020. Then it lost about 13% after July 2025.

Even some of the good years were rough. After the January 1992 and January 2001 runs, shares slid over 20% at one point before ending the year higher.

The July 2025 run started at a steep price

Microsoft's latest fast run hit the 50% mark the day after its fiscal 2025 fourth-quarter report on July 30, 2025. The July 31 close of $533.50 was around 50% over the April 8 low. Investors paid about 38 times earnings then, using the $14.13 a share Microsoft earned in fiscal 2025 on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis.

Story Continues

Shares drifted mostly sideways over a few months. Then they fell all the way to that $352.83 close on June 25, 2026 -- around 34% below where the run began.

Even a 15% gain the day after Microsoft's fiscal 2026 report in late July didn't erase the loss, and on July 31, 2026, shares were still about 13% down from a year earlier.

I'd say the starting price mattered more than the pace of the run. At around 38 times earnings, the shares could fall a long way on any hint of trouble.

Is this run different?

In a couple of ways, I think it is. Adjusted earnings per share grew 22% in fiscal 2026, and the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended Sept. 30, 2026) added another 18% gain, to $4.89. For the past four reported quarters, adjusted earnings were about $18.04 a share. At roughly $553, the stock costs about 31 times adjusted earnings, well under the 38 times earnings investors paid in July 2025.

Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing platform, is also accelerating. Its revenue climbed 40% year over year in the quarter that ended September 2025, then 42% in the quarter that ended this June and 48% in the last one.

Of course, that growth takes a lot of money. Microsoft's cash from operations rose 29% from a year ago. But free cash flow dropped about 27% to $18.6 billion as the company poured more cash into data centers.

What has Microsoft stock usually done after a run like this? It has usually kept rising. But that record only modestly beats the stock's odds in any given year, and the most recent case went the other way.

The business looks stronger than it did in July 2025, and the stock is cheaper relative to its earnings. Still, with free cash flow shrinking, paying about 31 times adjusted earnings just after a 57% run isn't something I'm eager to do.

news.Title: The AI Selloff Is Getting Worse. Nvidia, Dell and Data Center Stocks Are Plunging Hard. Is It Time to Buy the Dip?
news.Content:
Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence buildout fell broadly again in Thursday morning trading. On Wednesday, after Democrats swept the midterm elections, data-center builders and power-equipment makers fell as much as 20% or more, and Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL), optical-networking makers, and other AI hardware names dropped 7% to 10%, even as the S&P 500 rose. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) slipped about 3% and Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) about 5%.

But Thursday was worse for the biggest names. Nvidia's drop nearly doubled to about 6%, and Arm's to about 10%, and this time the broader market fell too, with the S&P 500 down about 1.5% as of roughly 9:55 a.m. ET. The builders and adjacent stocks hit hardest on Wednesday kept falling, though by less, with data-center cooling stock Modine (NYSE:MOD) down 9% after a 21% decline on Wednesday.

Which Stocks Fell?

Many big names felt quite a bit of damage. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom, fell about 6% to $188.75. Dell, one of the biggest sellers of AI servers, dropped about 9%, erasing about $20 billion in market value, and Arm lost about 10%, another roughly $20 billion. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR), server and component makers Hewlett Packard Enterprise (NYSE:HPE), and Celestica (NYSE:CLS) each fell 7% to 8%. Astera Labs (NASDAQ:ALAB), which makes chips that connect AI hardware inside data centers, slid about 11%.

Meanwhile, builders fell for a second day. Comfort Systems USA (NYSE:FIX), a mechanical and electrical contractor with heavy exposure to AI projects, fell about 9%. Argan (NYSE:AGX) lost about 9% and MasTec (NYSE:MTZ) about 8%, both pace for their second drop of 7% or more this month. EMCOR (NYSE:EME) and Dycom (NYSE:DY) were down 6% to 7%.

Also hard hit were optical-networking companies, which make the lasers and equipment that move data across fiber lines, including inside AI data centers. Ciena (NYSE:CIEN) fell about 11%, wiping out about $4.3 billion in value. Applied Optoelectronics (NASDAQ:AAOI) dropped about 13%, and Coherent (NYSE:COHR) and MACOM Technology (NASDAQ:MTSI) fell 9% to 11%.

Several companies that got their start in Bitcoin mining now build or rent out data centers for AI customers, and they fell too. Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD), which builds large data centers for AI workloads, fell about 11%. Core Scientific (NASDAQ:CORZ) and Cipher Digital lost roughly 8% to 9%. Meanwhile, Bitcoin itself was down only about 1% through about 10 a.m. ET, signaling that investors weren't selling these stocks over crypto. It wasn't until the broader market started tumbling that Bitcoin also started sliding, down nearly 6% by about 11 a.m. ET.

Story Continues

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Why the Midterms Matter for Data Centers

A big part of the worry is how quickly new data centers can be built, given the blue wave that swept through the Midterm elections. With Democrats now in charge of both chambers, investors are bracing for more oversight of an industry that many governments are already trying to regulate. In Texas, for example, one of the biggest data-center markets, the new governor-elect campaigned on pausing new data-center construction.

UBS analysts put a number on the risk: If construction pauses spread, they estimate that nearly a third of the new U.S. data-center capacity expected to come online in 2028 could be delayed or lost. For companies whose growth is contingent on the supply available to meet booming demand, that's a big deal.

Even Good News Isn't Helping

Perhaps the clearest example of how jumpy investors are is Viavi Solutions (NASDAQ:VIAV), which crashed 18% the morning after it reported that quarterly revenue jumped 57% to $469.3 million, raised its outlook, and approved a $500 million stock buyback.

The firm clearly delivered strong results, but the massive plunge shows the stock is trading on fear about the whole AI build-out rather than the business in particular. That could mean more pain if political news gets worse. But it can also mean the market is throwing out good companies along with the risky ones.

So, Is It Time to Buy the Dip?

For most investors, not all at once. The political risk is real but unsettled. Congress doesn't change hands until January, and any state-level pause would still have to be written and passed. Meanwhile, a 6% drop in Nvidia is a much smaller move than the double-digit losses in fiber makers or Wednesday's plunge in builders, a sign that investors are punishing the companies most exposed to new construction the hardest.

Some see value already. Asset manager VanEck argues the sell-off has left Bitcoin miners oversold because their access to the power grid is scarce and commands a premium for AI customers looking for places to build.

If you believe the AI build-out will keep going, a two-day plunge like this is the kind of moment long-term investors look for. The smarter move is to buy slowly, in pieces, and to favor companies with strong balance sheets and real customer contracts over the most speculative names. Just remember, these are among the most volatile AI stocks in the market right now. And if you'd rather avoid the political risk entirely, there are steadier ways to own tech stocks while Washington sorts this out.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »
